targetText:
Debt’s origins come from
 colonialism’s origins. Those who lend us money are those who
 colonized us. They are the same ones who used to manage our states and
 economies. These are the colonizers who indebted Africa through their
 brothers and cousins, who were the lenders. We had no connections with
 this debt. Therefore we cannot pay for it.
explanation: Sankara traces the material origins of third-world sovereign debt directly to European colonialism. The financial institutions and governments demanding debt servicing are the very powers that extracted Africa’s wealth for centuries, rendering foreign debt an odious continuation of colonial exploitation.

targetText:
Debt is neo-colonialism, in which
 colonizers have transformed themselves into “technical
 assistants.” We should rather say “technical assassins.” They
 present us with financing, with financial backers. As if someone’s
 backing could create development. We have been advised to go to these
 lenders. We have been offered nice financial arrangements. We have
 been indebted for 50, 60 years and even longer. That means we have
 been forced to compromise our people for over 50 years.
explanation: Highlighting how foreign aid and international financial loans function as imperialist leverage, Sankara exposes foreign technical assistance as structural domination that binds developing nations into multi-generational fiscal subservience.

targetText:
Under its current form, controlled
 and dominated by imperialism, debt is a skillfully managed reconquest
 of Africa, intended to subjugate its growth and development through
 foreign rules. Thus, each one of us becomes the financial slave, which
 is to say a true slave, of those who had been treacherous enough to
 put money in our countries with obligations for us to repay.
explanation: Sankara defines sovereign debt as a financial weapon of recolonization designed to dictate domestic economic policies, enforce structural adjustment, and ensure the continuous transfer of surplus value from the Global South to imperialist banks.

targetText:
Debt cannot be repaid, first
 because if we don’t repay, lenders will not die. That is for sure.
 But if we repay, we are going to die. That is also for sure. Those who
 led us to indebtedness gambled as if in a casino. As long as they had
 gains, there was no debate. But now that they suffer losses, they
 demand repayment. And we talk about crisis. No, Mister President, they
 played, they lost, that’s the rule of the game, and life goes on.
explanation: Contrasting speculative financial risk with the physical survival of working people, Sankara cuts through bourgeois moralism: if the debt is not repaid, wealthy lenders absorb minor losses; if repaid, millions of African workers and peasants face deprivation and death.

targetText:
It is our
 duty to create an Addis-Ababa united front against debt. That is the
 only way to assert that the refusal to repay is not an aggressive move
 on our part, but a fraternal move to speak the truth. Furthermore, the
 popular masses of Europe are not opposed to the popular masses of
 Africa. Those who want to exploit Africa are those who exploit Europe,
 too. We have a common enemy. So our Addis-Ababa Club will have to
 explain to each and all that debt shall not be repaid.
explanation: Sankara links African anti-colonial resistance to the struggles of European workers, articulating a unified class analysis: international finance capital exploits working people across continents, making collective solidarity and multilateral debt repudiation an urgent imperative.

targetText:
If Burkina Faso stands alone in
 refusing to pay, I will not be here for the next conference! But, with
 everyone’s support, which I need, with the support of everyone we
 would not have to pay. In doing so, we would devote our meager
 resources to our own development.
explanation: In a tragic and prophetic passage delivered less than three months before his assassination, Sankara warns that individual defiance against imperialist finance capital invites targeted elimination, demonstrating the vital necessity of collective continental solidarity.

targetText:
Let’s also make the African market be the
 market for Africans: produce in Africa, transform in Africa, consume
 in Africa. Let’s produce what we need and let’s consume what we
 produce instead of importing. Burkina Faso came here showing the
 cotton fabric produced in Burkina Faso, weaved in Burkina Faso, sown
 in Burkina Faso, to dress citizens of Burkina Faso.
explanation: Advocating practical socialist self-reliance, Sankara emphasizes agricultural and industrial autonomy: producing, transforming, and consuming domestic goods to break dependence on imperialist supply chains and empower local peasant weavers and workers.
